claims.text: A 2–5 micrometer Ti-based metallic-glass overlay can be deposited on the tailored Cantor alloy by laser cladding.
The overlay can be engineered with a compositional gradient at the interface with the Cantor alloy.
Laser cladding will produce a continuous, defect-free amorphous interfacial layer.
The compositional gradient will minimize thermal-expansion mismatch between the metallic glass and the underlying HEA.
The metallic-glass overlay will reduce interfacial phonon scattering.
The metallic-glass overlay will reduce interfacial electron scattering.
A smooth, well-adhered interface will facilitate heat transfer.
The compositional gradient will create a gradual transition in thermal-expansion properties.
The gradual transition in thermal-expansion properties will mitigate stress buildup during cyclic plasma heating.
The graded interface will reduce the risk of delamination during cyclic plasma heating.
The overlay will reduce interfacial thermal resistance relative to the unmodified Cantor-alloy intermediate layer.
Reduced interfacial thermal resistance will improve heat-transfer capability.
The coated intermediate layer will maintain or improve load-sharing mechanical integrity relative to the unmodified layer.
The current uncoated tailored Cantor-alloy intermediate layer has higher thermal resistance than the proposed coated layer.
The current uncoated intermediate layer is susceptible to structural degradation under repeated high-temperature plasma exposure.
The predicted improvement will hold during rapid thermal transients reaching approximately 1000°C.
The predicted improvement will hold under mechanical loads representative of plasma exposure.
Performance may change at temperatures or cycle counts beyond the tested range.
